PROJECT MISSION: SPATIAL RATIONALE
STRUCTURE: Merry Go Round

1. Footprint Analysis
The dimensions of this structure are 18 blocks wide (X), 11 blocks tall (Y), and 18 blocks deep (Z). The footprint is a perfect square, but the structure itself is a tiered, radially symmetric cylinder. It is mostly hollow on the inside to accommodate the ride's interior, featuring a solid mechanical base and roof, with an open midsection for the carousel poles. A bounding box marker is present at the extreme corners (0,0 and 17,17) extending vertically, which I will use to keep my spatial alignment perfectly square while building a circular object.

2. Material Strategy
I will use Grass Block and Dirt for the foundation to ground the structure in a park-like setting. The Dirt will specifically be used to draw a worn, circular path where foot traffic has trampled the grass. 
I will use Oak Planks for the boarding deck; wood provides a warm, realistic boardwalk feel for the riders. 
I will use Iron Blocks for the heavy mechanical components—specifically the rotating floor disk and the ceiling gear disk. 
I will use Stone for the structural elements: the four outer support pillars, the vertical carousel poles, the stylized horses, and the sloped roof canopy. Stone provides a rigid contrast to the iron and wood. 
Finally, I will use White Wool for decorative accents, central axis markers, and the bounding box guideposts.

3. Construction Sequence & Logic
At Y=0 (The Foundation): I will lay down an 18x18 grassy park base. I will carve a circular dirt path into the grass to represent the trampled ground where visitors walk around the ride. I will place white wool at the opposite corners to establish my absolute boundaries.

At Y=1 (The Boarding Platform): I will build an elevated, hollow ring of Oak Planks. This is the wooden deck where riders step up to board. I will place four Stone blocks at the outer corners of the platform to serve as the base for the structural pillars that will hold up the roof. I will also place a White Wool block in the exact center (X=9, Z=9) to mark the central rotation axis.

At Y=2 (The Mechanical Floor): I will construct a large, solid disk of Iron Blocks. This represents the heavy, rotating metal floor of the merry-go-round. I will continue the four outer Stone pillars upward.

At Y=3 to Y=5 (The Ride Interior): I am now building the core of the carousel. I will place Stone blocks in a circular, spaced-out pattern to represent the vertical poles and the stylized horses attached to them. I will mix in White Wool to add decorative details to the horses and the central pillar. The outer Stone support pillars continue to rise.

At Y=6 (The Upper Mechanism): I will continue the poles, but I will thicken the central axis with Stone and Wool. I must do this to visually support the heavy mechanical roof that is about to be placed on top.

At Y=7 (The Canopy Base): I will mirror the iron disk from Y=2, creating another large Iron Block circle. This acts as the mechanical ceiling that houses the upper gears and holds the poles from above.

At Y=8 (The Roof Rim): I will use Stone to build a hollow, circular ring resting on the outer edge of the iron canopy. This forms the sloped, tent-like roof of the carousel, tapering inward.

At Y=9 (The Roof Peak): I will place a single Stone block in the dead center of the roof to cap the canopy and bring the slope to a point.

At Y=10 (The Finial): I will top the entire structure with a single White Wool block at the center, acting as a decorative flag or finial to complete the merry-go-round. I will also place the final bounding box marker at the corner.

I am building an 'American-style Tractor Head', which is the iconic, long-hooded semi-truck cab. 

Footprint Analysis:
The dimensions of this build are 13 blocks in length (X=0 to X=12), 5 blocks in width (Z=0 to Z=4), and 5 blocks in height (Y=0 to Y=4). The structure is solid at its core but highly tiered. It features a low, long front hood, a tall central sleeper cab, and a flat, low rear chassis designed to hold a trailer. 

Material Strategy:
I will use Stone (A) as my primary heavy material for the tires, engine block, and main cab walls to give the truck a rugged, industrial weight. I will use Stone Slabs (B) extensively to sculpt the vehicle's aerodynamics—creating low-clearance chassis floors, curved wheel fenders, and sloped roof fairings. I will use regular Glass (C) for the windshield and driver's side windows. I will use White Stained Glass (D) along the sides of the sleeper cab to represent classic painted truck stripes or frosted sleeper windows. Finally, I will use Iron Blocks (E) to construct the massive, gleaming vertical exhaust stacks that are signature to American semi-trucks.

Construction Sequence & Logic:
At Y=0, I will establish the chassis and wheelbase. I will run a solid spine of Stone Slabs straight down the center (Z=2) from X=1 to X=12. To form the front steering axle, I will place Stone blocks wide at X=2 (Z=0 and Z=4). For the heavy-duty rear axles, I will place Stone blocks slightly tighter to the body at X=11 and X=12 (Z=1 and Z=3). I will fill the gaps with slabs to create the fifth-wheel hitch area and low undercarriage.

At Y=1, I will build the engine block and cab floor. At the very front (X=0, Z=2), I will place a single Stone block to act as the protruding front bumper. Behind it, I will build out the long engine hood (X=1 to X=3), using slabs on the outer edges to form the front wheel fenders. From X=4 to X=8, I will lay down a solid block of Stone to form the heavy floor and lower walls of the driver's cabin and rear sleeper unit. The rear chassis (X=9 to X=12) remains empty from this layer up to allow space for a trailer to attach.

At Y=2, I will shape the upper body and greenhouse (windows). I will place slabs over the engine block to slope the hood downward for visibility. At X=3 and X=4, I will install the Glass windshield and side windows to enclose the driver's seat. Moving back along the sleeper cab (X=5 to X=7), I will embed White Stained Glass into the Stone walls to create a sleek, decorative side stripe. At the rear corners of the cab (X=8, Z=1 and Z=3), I will place my first Iron Blocks to anchor the heavy vertical exhaust stacks.

At Y=3, I will cap the cabin and extend the exhausts. I will place Stone Slabs at the front of the roof (X=3 and X=4) to continue the aerodynamic upward slope from the windshield. I will use solid Stone to roof the sleeper section behind it. At X=8, I will place another set of Iron Blocks on top of the previous ones, pushing the smokestacks high above the driver's window line.

At Y=4, I will complete the truck's aerodynamics. I will build a wind deflector (fairing) on the very top rear of the sleeper cab (X=7 and X=8) using a combination of slabs and stone. I should do this to visually bridge the height gap between the truck cab and a standard cargo trailer, completing the classic, wedge-like silhouette of an American highway hauler.

As a Master Teacher, I will guide you through the spatial visualization of the 'Slime Farm Schematic With Spawner'. Before you look at the raw coordinates, I want you to build this structure in your mind's eye. 

1. Footprint Analysis
I am working with a bounding box that is 15 blocks wide (X=0 to 14), 15 blocks deep (Z=0 to 14), and 14 blocks tall (Y=0 to 13). This is not a uniform cube; it is a tiered, hollow structure. It resembles a giant funnel or mushroom. The bottom half is a narrow 5x5 pillar acting as a collection and kill chamber, which abruptly expands at Y=5 into a wide 13x13 floating room where the slimes will spawn. You will notice single stone blocks at the extreme opposite corners of the schematic (Y=0, X=14, Z=0 and Y=13, X=0, Z=14); I will use these simply as bounding box markers to anchor the blueprint.

2. Material Strategy
I will use a highly functional palette tailored for a mob farm:
- Stone (A): I will use this as my primary structural anchor. It will form the foundation, the opaque walls of the lower chute, the massive floor of the spawning room, and the placeholder blocks for the spawner itself.
- Chest (B): I will place a double chest at the very bottom to collect the slimeballs.
- Glass (C): I will use glass extensively for the walls of the upper spawning chamber and the front viewing window of the kill chamber. Glass is transparent, preventing unwanted mob spawns on the walls while allowing me to monitor the farm's efficiency.
- Water (D): I will use water for two distinct mechanical purposes: as a drowning column in the lower chute (since slimes sink and drown), and as a horizontal flushing system in the upper chamber to push slimes into the chute.

3. Construction Sequence
Let's build this layer by layer.

Y=0 (The Foundation & Storage): I will start by placing my double chest at the front (X=7, Z=3 and 4). Just behind it, I will lay down a solid 5x5 Stone foundation (X=5 to 9, Z=5 to 9). This is the base of our kill chamber.

Y=1 to Y=3 (The Drowning Chute): I will build the walls of the 5x5 chute. I will use Stone for the back and side walls, but for the front wall (facing the chests), I will use Glass so I can watch the slimes drown. Inside this chute, I will leave a 3x3 hollow core and fill it completely with Water. 

Y=4 (The Chute Seal): I will continue the 3x3 water column, but I will replace the front Glass wall with solid Stone. I am doing this to reinforce the top of the pillar, preparing it to hold the massive floor above.

Y=5 (The Spawning Floor): I will dramatically expand my footprint. I will build a solid 13x13 Stone platform centered over the chute. This acts as the floor of the upper spawning chamber and blocks light from reaching the kill chamber below.

Y=6 to Y=7 (The Flushing System): I will begin constructing the outer walls of the spawning chamber using Glass, reinforcing the corners with Stone. Inside, I will create a water conveyor belt. At Y=6, I will place water across the floor, leaving a 3x3 hole in the exact center (X=6 to 8, Z=6 to 8) that drops directly into the drowning chute. At Y=7, I will place water source blocks only along the outer edges. This creates a flowing current that pushes any spawned slimes directly into the center hole.

Y=8 to Y=11 (The Spawning Chamber): I will build the Glass walls up for four more layers, leaving the entire 11x11 interior completely hollow (filled with air). I must provide this 4-block high clearance because large slimes require a 3-block high space to spawn and jump without suffocating.

Y=12 to Y=13 (The Spawner & Roof): I will finish the top of the Glass walls. In the exact dead center of the room (X=7, Z=7), suspended in the air above the water hole, I will place a Stone block at Y=12, capped by another at Y=13. I will use this central pillar as the mounting point for the Slime Spawner. By placing it high in the center, slimes will spawn in mid-air, drop into the flowing water, and be swept down into the drowning chute below.

Footprint Analysis. I am looking at a structure that is 7 blocks wide on the X axis, 7 blocks deep on the Z axis, and 6 blocks tall on the Y axis. The footprint is a nearly perfect square, but because this is a makeshift Tardis, the overall volume is highly irregular. It begins as a solid, heavy base, transitions into a chaotic and hollow midsection, and tapers off into an asymmetrical partial roof.

Material Strategy. I will use Stone as the primary building block. Stone provides a heavy, brutalist, and improvised feel, perfect for a makeshift or crashed machine rather than the sleek wood of a real police box. I will use White Stained Glass sparingly to represent the iconic Tardis light and the internal console glow. The glass will form a vertical pillar, acting as the energetic core of this crude replica.

Construction Sequence. 
At Y=0 and Y=1, I will lay down a thick, two-block-high foundation of nearly solid Stone. I will intentionally leave a few corners empty to give the base a chipped, weathered appearance. This solid mass will anchor the structure to the ground.

At Y=2, I will begin constructing the walls, but I will make them jagged and unpredictable. I will leave hollow gaps throughout the layer to create a cramped, broken interior. At the coordinates X=3, Z=4, I will place my first block of White Stained Glass, embedding it within the stone to start the glowing central core.

At Y=3, I will build the walls higher but keep the interior mostly hollow. I will wrap Stone tightly around the White Stained Glass block, framing it like a crude window or a makeshift control panel that emits a white glow.

At Y=4, I will drastically thin out the outer shell. I will concentrate the Stone blocks along the northern and eastern edges to form a protective, asymmetrical shroud. I will extend the White Stained Glass pillar upward, leaving it partially exposed to the open air to simulate a broken casing.

At Y=5, I will reinforce the northern edge with a solid line of Stone to create a partial roof overhang. I will place the final block of White Stained Glass at the top of the central pillar. This serves as the makeshift version of the iconic roof lamp, glowing amidst the ruined stone shell.

At Y=6, I will leave the layer entirely empty of blocks, finalizing the structure's height and completing the makeshift Tardis.

Welcome, student. Today we are constructing a 'Médiéval House'. To master this build, you must look past the raw coordinates and understand the architectural intent. Let us walk through the spatial logic together.

Footprint Analysis:
The bounding box for this build is a 21x21 square on the X and Z axes, reaching 17 blocks high (Y=0 to Y=16). The structure itself is hollow and tiered, consisting of two intersecting geometric volumes: a large, roughly octagonal main living space, and a smaller rectangular wing extending toward the South-East. 

Material Strategy:
I will use Stone (A) as my primary load-bearing material. It will form the foundation, the structural pillars, the roof edging, and the chimneys, giving the house a heavy, grounded medieval feel. I will use Oak Planks (B) for the floors and to fill the spaces between the stone pillars, creating a classic wattle-and-daub or timber-framed illusion. I will use Grass Blocks (D) strategically on the exterior as window planter boxes to add life to the facade. I will use Stone Slabs (E) to create a gently sloping, finished roof. Finally, the Glass blocks (C) you see at the extreme diagonal corners (Y=0 and Y=16) are not part of the house; I am using them purely as invisible bounding box markers to define the 3D workspace.

Construction Sequence & Logic:
At Y=0, I will lay the foundation. I will outline the octagonal main room and the rectangular wing using Stone to ensure the base is protected from ground moisture. I will also place my first Glass marker in the corner.

At Y=1, I will lay the ground floor. I will fill the entire interior footprint with solid Oak Planks to create a warm, walkable surface.

From Y=2 to Y=5, I will raise the first-floor walls, keeping the interior hollow. I will alternate Stone and Oak Planks in a specific pattern (ABAABABAABA). I am doing this to simulate vertical timber framing, a hallmark of medieval architecture. At Y=2, I will place clusters of Grass Blocks on the outside edges of the walls; these will serve as exterior window planter boxes.

At Y=6, I will construct the ceiling of the first floor, which doubles as the floor for the second story. I will fill the interior space with solid Oak Planks again, and I will add another set of Grass Blocks to serve as second-story planters.

From Y=7 to Y=9, I will build the second-story walls. I will continue the hollow interior and maintain the alternating Stone and Oak pattern to carry the timber-frame aesthetic upward.

At Y=10, I will begin the roof transition. I will flare the Stone blocks outward by one block around the entire perimeter. I am doing this to create the roof eaves—an overhang that will provide shade and shed rainwater away from the wooden walls below.

At Y=11 and Y=12, I will step the walls inward, tapering the roof of both the main octagonal tower and the rectangular wing. 

At Y=13, I will cap the roof. I will use Stone Slabs across the top of the tapered walls. I am using slabs here instead of full blocks to give the roof a smooth, shallow pitch that finishes the structure elegantly.

At Y=14, I will place a few isolated Stone blocks on top of the roof slabs. I am adding these to serve as chimneys and decorative roof finials to break up the flat silhouette of the roofline.

Layer Y=15 is left empty to give the chimneys breathing room, and at Y=16, I will place my final Glass block in the opposite corner to close out the bounding box. 

By visualizing these intersecting shapes and understanding the purpose of the timber-frame pattern and roof overhangs, you can now build this Médiéval House with perfect spatial awareness.

I want the observer to feel dwarfed by this blank, bone-white canvas.

- Oak Logs (C): I will use these as the primary structural skeleton—vertical pillars at the corners and horizontal tie-beams between floors.

Y=0 (Foundation):
I will lay down the L-shaped foundation. I will place Oak Logs at the structural corners and fill the primary wall lines with Cobblestone. I will wrap the exterior base with Stone and Stone Slabs to create a solid, stepped footing that anchors the house to the ground.

Y=1 to Y=2 (First Floor Walls):
I will build the first-floor walls upward. I will switch the main wall material from Cobblestone to smooth Stone to create a cleaner look for the living space. I will continue driving the Oak Log pillars straight up at the corners. The interior remains completely hollow.

Y=3 (The Ring Beam):
I will cap the first floor. I will lay a continuous horizontal ring of Oak Logs directly on top of the stone walls. This acts as a structural tie-beam. I will line the outside of this log beam with Stone Slabs to create a visual divider between the first and second floors.

Y=4 (The Jetty / Second Floor Overhang):
I will begin the second floor. To achieve a classic medieval look, I will "jetty" (overhang) the second floor. I will push the footprint outward by one block in several directions. Because this floor needs to be lighter, I will switch the primary wall material to Oak Planks, while maintaining the Oak Log corners. I will use Stone and Stone Slabs on the very outer edges to support this overhang.

Y=7 (Eaves and Roof Base):

Y=0: The Foundation and Floor
